what_its_for: Elacestrant is a cancer medicine used to treat a certain type of breast cancer in adults who have already gone through menopause (or in men with breast cancer). It is used when your cancer has spread to other parts of the body (metastatic) and your cancer cells have a specific protein called the estrogen receptor (ER-positive) but do NOT have the HER2 protein (HER2-negative). It is also used when your cancer has a change (mutation) in a gene called ESR1. Your doctor will test your cancer cells to make sure this medicine is right for you. Elacestrant is typically used after at least one other hormonal therapy has already been tried.
how_to_take: Swallow the tablets whole with water. You can take elacestrant with food or without food, but taking it with food (a meal or snack) may help prevent nausea and stomach upset. Do not crush, chew, or split the tablets. Take this medicine at around the same time every day to help you remember. If you vomit after taking your dose, do NOT take an extra tablet — just take your next dose at the regular scheduled time.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 345 mg (which is typically three 115 mg tablets) taken by mouth once daily. Your doctor may lower your dose if you have certain side effects or other health conditions such as liver problems. Always follow the exact dose your doctor prescribed — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember ON THE SAME DAY. If you do not remember until the next day, skip the missed dose completely and just take your regular dose that day. Never take two doses in one day to make up for a missed dose.
storage: Store your tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep them away from moisture and heat. Store in the original container with the cap tightly closed. Keep this medicine out of the reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of leftover medicine.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking certain medicines that can interact with elacestrant without first talking to your doctor or pharmacist. These include some antibiotics (like rifampin), some seizure medicines (like carbamazepine or phenytoin), some antifungal medicines (like itraconazole or ketoconazole), some HIV medicines, and St. John's Wort (a herbal supplement). Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice, as these can increase the amount of medicine in your blood and raise your risk of side effects. Do not become pregnant while taking this medicine — it can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 1 week after your last dose. If you are breastfeeding, talk to your doctor, as you should not breastfeed while taking this medicine.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away or seek emergency help if you experience any of the following: severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that does not go away or is affecting your ability to eat or drink; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice), dark urine, severe stomach pain, or unusual tiredness; bone pain that is new or gets worse; shortness of breath or chest pain; signs of high cholesterol or high triglycerides (your doctor will monitor this with blood tests); any unusual or severe symptoms you are worried about. Tell your doctor about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you are taking before starting elacestrant.
when_it_works: Elacestrant works by blocking estrogen receptors on cancer cells, which helps slow down or stop the growth of cancer. It does not cure cancer, but it is designed to help keep the cancer from growing. You may not feel any different at first. Your doctor will check how well the medicine is working through scans and other tests over time. It is important to keep taking your medicine every day even if you feel well.
special_populations: Older adults (age 65 and older): This medicine has been studied in older adults and can be used, but your doctor will monitor you closely for side effects. Liver problems: If you have moderate liver problems, your doctor will likely lower your dose. Elacestrant is not recommended if you have severe liver problems. Kidney problems: No dose change is usually needed for mild to moderate kidney problems, but tell your doctor about any kidney issues. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do NOT take this medicine if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant — it can cause serious harm to an unborn baby. Women who could become pregnant must use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 1 week after the last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine. Men with breast cancer: This medicine can be used in men with breast cancer under the same conditions as women.
